---
title: "Dice and Decks: Does the Generator Remember?"
---

Place a fair six-sided die beside six cards labeled $1$ through $6$. Shuffle the cards uniformly.

Before the first observation, either object produces each label with probability $1/6$.

Now observe a six.

What remains possible depends on what we do with the card.

## 🔰 Replacement is a rule of the experiment {#sec-sample-dice-and-decks-replacement-is-a-rule-of-the-experiment}

For the ideal die, assume each roll is independent and fair. Its next six still has probability $1/6$.

For the cards, there are two procedures:

- **Replace and randomize again.** Put the card back and choose uniformly again. With independent choices, the next draw has the same law as the first.
- **Keep the card out.** The remaining deck contains no six. The next draw cannot be six.

The original alphabet and first-draw probabilities were identical. The update rule changed the sequence.

## 🏵 A deck carries an inventory {#sec-sample-dice-and-decks-a-deck-carries-an-inventory}

Let $c_t[f]$ count cards labeled $f$ just before draw $t$. If each remaining card is equally likely to be selected, then

$$
p_t[f]=\frac{c_t[f]}{\sum_g c_t[g]}.
$$

After drawing label $v$ without replacement,

$$
c_{t+1}[f]=c_t[f]-\mathbf1_{\{f=v\}}.
$$

The indicator $\mathbf1_{\{f=v\}}$ is one when $f=v$ and zero otherwise. Only the emitted label loses a card.

For a deck with two copies of every face, the first probability of six is $2/12$. After drawing a six, the second is $1/11$. The profile changes because the source has been consumed.

After the final card, drawing is undefined until we specify a reset or replenishment rule.

## ⚙️ Compare two observations {#sec-sample-dice-and-decks-compare-two-observations}

Two sixes from the independent die have probability

$$
\frac16\cdot\frac16=\frac1{36}.
$$

Two sixes from the six-card deck without replacement have probability zero.

For a six followed by a five, the deck gives

$$
\frac16\cdot\frac15=\frac1{30}.
$$

The second denominator is five because the second choice is made from a smaller inventory.

The multiplication follows the order of the experiment: first six, then five among the cards that remain.

## 💡 A run can carry a guarantee that one draw cannot {#sec-sample-dice-and-decks-a-run-can-carry-a-guarantee-that-one-draw-cannot}

Drawing all six cards guarantees one appearance of each face. Six die rolls supply no such guarantee.

For the die, the probability of at least one six in six independent rolls is

$$
1-\left(\frac56\right)^6\approx0.665.
$$

There is still about a one-in-three chance of seeing no six. “One chance in six” has never promised one occurrence in every block of six.

Conversely, a particular card in a uniformly shuffled deck has probability $1/6$ of occupying any fixed position. Its marginal probabilities look uniform across positions even though the draws depend on one another.

## ☯ The observation may change the source {#sec-sample-dice-and-decks-the-observation-may-change-the-source}

This distinction travels beyond games. Sampling units from a finite population without replacement, consuming stock from a warehouse, and drawing independent simulated values require different models.

The generator's state tells us whether repetition offers a fresh version of the same trial.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-dice-and-decks-try-the-idea}

A deck contains two red and two blue cards. Draw without replacement. After observing red, what is the chance of another red? What would it be with replacement and independent randomization?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-dice-and-decks-work-it-through}

Without replacement, one red remains among three cards, giving $1/3$. With replacement, two red remain among four, giving $1/2$. The first observation changes the next inventory only in the first procedure.
:::
